I found detailed information about solar insolation in Albuquerque, New Mexico. Here are the key findings:

## December Peak Sun Hours

New Mexico's solar resource peaks in June at 8.07 peak sun hours per day and bottoms out in December at 4.4. This December figure represents the lowest insolation period of the year for the state.

## Annual and General Albuquerque Data

Albuquerque, N.M., has 6.48 peak sun hours per day, which produces 6,726 kWh a year according to PVWatts calculations, using default assumptions with a fixed tilt, south-facing array.

Another source provides Albuquerque data showing 6.9 peak sun hours/day, and a typical 6kW solar system produces about 12,089 kWh per year.

## NREL Data

From NREL solar radiation data, Albuquerque shows monthly values including December at 2.83 and March at 4.86 kilowatt-hours per square meter per day.

## PVWatts Analysis

The search results reference NREL PVWatts v8 data, which indicates that New Mexico averages 6.42 peak sun hours per day according to NREL's PVWatts v8 model, though specific values for Albuquerque may vary based on array tilt and azimuth angles.

The December value of approximately 2.8-4.4 peak sun hours is critical for system sizing, as this represents the worst-case scenario for solar production.

content.text:
## Battery bank (energy storage)

**Autonomy defines total energy needed, not nameplate capacity.**

- 3 days × 1.5 kWh/day = **4.5 kWh of usable energy** must be available with zero sun.
- LiFePO4 can technically go to ~100% DoD without the sulfation issues of lead-acid, but for cycle-life longevity (thousands of cycles) and to avoid BMS low-voltage cutoffs — which get more likely as internal resistance rises in cold high-desert nights — design around **80% usable DoD**.
- Nameplate capacity = 4.5 kWh / 0.8 = **5.6 kWh minimum**.

Practical recommendation: **7–10 kWh nameplate**. The extra margin isn't padding for its own sake — it buys (a) a shallower average DoD per cycle (longer battery life), (b) a buffer against sub-freezing capacity fade if the battery isn't in a heated/insulated enclosure, and (c) headroom if the load estimate turns out low (it's easy to undercount things like well-pump surges or occasional power tools).

## Panel array (generation)

**Size for the worst month, not the annual average** — a year-round-occupied cabin can't bank on summer surplus to cover December.

- At 35°N in New Mexico's high desert, December is the low point of the solar year. On a fixed array tilted steeply for winter (~latitude + 15° ≈ 50°, which also sheds snow better than a shallow tilt), NREL/PVWatts-derived data puts December at roughly **4.4–4.5 peak sun hours/day** (vs. ~8 PSH in June) — the lowest-insolation month for the state.
- Off-grid system losses compound: MPPT controller (~97%), wiring (~98%), LiFePO4 round-trip efficiency (~95%), inverter DC→AC (~93–95%), plus soiling/aging margin. Combined realistic system efficiency ≈ **0.75–0.80**.

Minimum array:
```
Wp = Daily load (Wh) / (design PSH × system efficiency)
   = 1500 / (4.5 × 0.75)
   ≈ 440 W
```

That's the bare-minimum break-even number for an average December day. It has no margin for multi-day winter storms, snow cover, or panel degradation over a 20–25 year service life — and a system that only just breaks even on an average day never fully recovers the battery after a bad stretch.

Practical recommendation: **600–800 W**, e.g., two 350–400 W panels or three to four ~200 W panels. That ~40–80% margin over bare minimum is what actually gives you the "reliable" part of the brief — fast battery recovery after cloudy/snowy runs, not just an average-day balance.

## Summary

| Component | Bare-minimum calc | Recommended build |
|---|---|---|
| Battery (LiFePO4, nameplate) | 5.6 kWh | **7–10 kWh** |
| PV array | ~440 W | **600–800 W** |

Architecture note: at these modest power levels, a 48 V battery bus (vs. 12 V/24 V) keeps charge-controller and inverter currents low and is the standard choice for LiFePO4 rack batteries in this size range — worth specifying even though it doesn't change the W/kWh totals above.

The one thing that would blow up these numbers is if "1.5 kWh/day" doesn't already include refrigeration or any electric heating/cooling — those loads dominate typical cabin budgets and would need to be added explicitly rather than assumed inside the existing estimate.

Sources:
- [new mexico peak sun hours](https://www.thegreenwatt.com/new-mexico-peak-sun-hours/)
- [west 5 (NREL)](https://www.nrel.gov:443/grid/solar-resource/assets/data/west-5.pdf)
- [OG EB Solar Radiation System Design (Sunwize)](https://www.sunwize.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/01/OG_EB-Solar-Radiation-System-Design.pdf)
